originalTitle: Thar she blows! Hull Maritime Museum resurfaces with a walk-in whale and a ‘monkey mermaid’
summary: The £20m reboot shows off exhibits ranging from a giant whale skeleton to tiny ‘scrimshaws’ of carved bone to a very strange mermaid, all telling a gripping tale of a great seafaring city
content: The star attraction of Hull’s revamped and revitalised Maritime Museum is a colossal 40ft-long skeleton of an North Atlantic right whale, beached more than a century ago. The remains of this leviathan dominate an exhibition space scarcely large enough to contain its stupendous bulk. Children can crawl into its ribcage, like junior Jonahs, popping up in a clear plastic dome as digital images of swimming whales slowly unspool across the ceiling. Docile, leisurely and extremely blubbery – which meant that harpooned carcasses conveniently floated, as well as yielding copious quantities of valuable oil – the North Atlantic right whale was hunted almost to extinction during the whaling era. Today, it’s estimated that there are fewer than 400 left. At the other end of the cetacean scale is a delicately carved whale that can fit into the palm of your hand, studded with miniature harpoons designed for use as toothpicks. It forms part of the museum’s world class collection of scrimshaw, the niche and intensely fiddly folk art of carving and decorating pieces of ivory or bone. Crewmen would while away the long hours “scrimshandering”, inscribing whales’ teeth and walrus tusks with images of ships and patriotic Britannias, or tableaux from their travels and portraits of loved ones. Other bounties on display include the spiralled rapiers of narwhal tusks, surreally fashioned into hatstands and bedposts. Hull’s geography ensured that its history was indisputably maritime. Set at the confluence of the River Hull and Humber estuary, it prospered, successively, through trading, whaling and fishing. Latterly, its historic relationship with the sea has been renewed through the production of wind turbine blades for offshore arrays at the city’s Alexandra Dock. And Hull and the Humber remain one of the UK’s busiest port complexes. Nonetheless, the sense of city out on a limb, and one that has seen better days, still persists. Hull’s centre is pockmarked with vacant shops, and its docklands, which took a pounding during the second world war, remain apologetically gap-toothed in places, despite the crowded marina and upscale warehouse conversions. The poet Philip Larkin, Hull’s most infamous adopted son, who measured out his life in coffee spoons as head librarian of the city’s university, wrote of “the surprise of a large town … where only salesmen and relations come, within a terminate and fishy-smelling pastoral of ships up streets ...” Larkin had an ambivalent relationship with Hull, but a statue of him, erected in 2010, now greets you at the city’s Paragon station. When the dock offices first opened in 1871, Larkin’s “pastoral of ships up streets” would have been an even more emphatic reality. At that time, Hull’s skyline was more ships’ masts than church spires, with vessels crammed into a network of docks. Set on a prominent site overlooking the now infilled Queen’s Dock, the dock offices exude a chest-puffing, Victorian mercantile bombast. Originally designed by Christopher Wray, whose career encompassed a spell in Calcutta’s public works department, the building’s florid and fruity neoclassical style is embellished with Neptunian details such as sea monsters, fishing nets and trident-like railings. An unconventional triangular plan was crowned by chunky pepperpot cupolas at its three corners. Now listed Grade II*, it was converted into the city’s Maritime Museum in 1975. (The museum itself began life in 1912 as the more prosaic Museum of Fisheries and Shipping in the city’s Pickering Park.) Over time, however, the Museum of Hull, as it was known, became tired, shabby and ripe for a reboot. Only two of its four floors were publicly accessible and the main exhibition space was painted shiny grey and lurid Germolene pink. “You also couldn’t read the whole room as a volume because there was this big ramp in the middle going up to a mezzanine level,” says Claire Humphrey, senior architect with conservation specialist Purcell, which oversaw the remodelling. The intrusive ramp has been removed and the colour scheme toned down to a more historically accurate and visually palatable palette: subtle marine blues set against a glacially white ceiling. The £20.4m project follows on from Hull’s successful stint as City of Culture in 2017. Funding came jointly from Hull city council, which contributed £11.8mn, along with the National Lottery Heritage Fund, which allocated £7.7m. The remainder was raised through private donations. The rebooting has enabled the museum to double its public space and show 50% more objects from its expansive collection. Around 1,300 artefacts are now on display across the galleries and open storage spaces, many being seen by the public for the first time. Underscored by a reframed approach to curation, new display systems bring Hull’s maritime cornucopia more vividly to life, from dockers’ tools and a stuffed polar bear, to Inuit bootees and a so-called “mermaid” (actually a rather hideous chimera of a monkey fused with a fish). A veritable regatta of model ships, pedantically accurate to the last detail, illustrates the shift from sail to steam, an advance that supercharged the shipping and fishing industries. One of the museum’s most cherished artefacts is a carved wooden figurehead of a bounding dog from the Sirius, the first steamship to complete a transatlantic crossing entirely under steam power in 1838. Other sections explore the rich currents of migration that flowed through Hull, propitiously poised between Old and New Worlds. You can also learn about Lillian Bilocca, the “headscarf revolutionary” who doughtily campaigned to improve safety on fishing fleets in the 1960s. In 150 years of commercial trawling out of Hull, more than 6,000 crewmen were lost, now commemorated in the museum’s simple and dignified memorial space. chineseTitle: 她吹了！赫尔海事博物馆重新亮相，展出一头步入式鲸鱼和一条“猴美人鱼”
chineseSummary: 耗资 2000 万英镑的重新启动展示了各种展品，从巨型鲸鱼骨架到微型骨雕“骷髅”，再到非常奇怪的美人鱼，所有这些都讲述了一个伟大的航海城市的扣人心弦的故事
chineseContent: 经过改造和复兴的赫尔海事博物馆的明星景点是一具 40 英尺长的巨大北大西洋露脊鲸骨架，它于一个多世纪前搁浅。这个庞然大物的遗骸占据了一个几乎不足以容纳其巨大体积的展览空间。孩子们可以像小乔纳一样爬进它的胸腔，在透明的塑料圆顶中突然出现，而鲸鱼游泳的数字图像在天花板上慢慢地展开。北大西洋露脊鲸性情温顺、悠闲、极其多脂——这意味着用鱼叉捕获的鲸鱼尸体可以方便地漂浮，并能产出大量有价值的石油——在捕鲸时代，北大西洋露脊鲸几乎被猎杀至灭绝。如今，估计只剩下不到 400 人。鲸类鳞片的另一端是一头精雕细琢的鲸鱼，大小可放入手掌，上面镶嵌着设计用作牙签的微型鱼叉。它是博物馆世界级的雕饰收藏的一部分，雕饰是用象牙或骨头雕刻和装饰的小众而极其精致的民间艺术。船员们会通过“刻画”来消磨长时间的工作，在鲸鱼的牙齿和海象牙上刻上船只和爱国不列颠尼亚号的图像，或者在旅行中拍摄的场景和亲人的肖像。展出的其他赏金包括独角鲸象牙的螺旋细剑，它们被超现实地塑造成帽架和床柱。赫尔的地理位置确保了其无可争议的海洋历史。它位于赫尔河和亨伯河口的交汇处，先后通过贸易、捕鲸和捕鱼而繁荣起来。最近，通过在该市的亚历山德拉码头生产用于海上阵列的风力涡轮机叶片，它与海洋的历史关系得到了更新。还有赫尔和亨伯雷迈
